documents.abstract: This chapter addresses one of the most sensitive areas in occupational health practice: supporting employees who are experiencing depression and assessing concerns about suicide. It begins by exploring how depressive symptoms influence work participation, functional capacity and decision-making, and how workplace pressures may contribute to the onset or worsening of mental distress. It also outlines how occupational health practitioners can support safe work retention and facilitate a sustainable return to work. The chapter then describes a structured approach to mental health assessment using validated tools such as the Patient Health Questionnaire-9, the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 and the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale. These instruments inform, but do not determine, clinical reasoning. A formulation-led method is presented that reflects contemporary guidance promoting personalised assessment, collaborative safety planning and a move away from predictive or stratified risk approaches. Finally, the chapter considers the emotional impact of repeated exposure to distress on occupational health practitioners. It highlights the importance of supervision, reflective practice and structured decompression as preventive supports. The aim is to provide clear, evidence-informed guidance to strengthen assessment, communication, documentation and practitioner well-being within occupational health practice.

The current study, which is entitled Evaluating the Assessing the Acceptance of ChatGPT Among Higher Education Students: A Case Study in Pahang, aimed to assess the behavioural intention of university students with regard to using ChatGPT in various academic levels. The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) was selected as a cross-sectional survey approach, data were collected from 184 respondents between March and May 2025 through both online and printed questionnaires. The core antecedents included in the analysis were the performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, habit, and personal innovativeness and were operationalised using a five-point Likert scale. Descriptive analysis revealed an overall mean behavioural intention score of 3.523 (SD = 0.901), indicating a generally positive inclination toward ChatGPT adoption. Notably, both bachelor and postgraduate students erred higher mean scores (4.400 and 4.370, respectively) in comparison with students of the foundation level (3.393), which suggests that students of higher learning level assign AI-based technologies a higher academic rating. These results highlight an increasing openness to generative AI among the population of higher education, and at the same time, they indicate the presence of strong inequalities among the academic layers. Therefore, the findings reinforce the need to introduce specific AI-literacy programmes and responsible digital education to facilitate fair and responsible usage. Despite the methodological constraints, such as sampling, and the disproportional number of groups, the generalisability of the findings is diluted but still, the study provides useful information to the growing discourse on AI implementation into higher education, at least in the developing regional milieus. Moreover, the study presents practical research implications to institutions of higher education working to come up with evidence-based, inclusionary, and ethically sustainable strategies to implement ChatGPT and other similar technologies in pedagogical and curricular contexts.

Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming quality assurance in higher education by enabling adaptive, data-driven assessments of teaching performance and student learning. This integrative review synthesizes the purposes, methodologies, and outcomes of AI-enabled assessments, examines emerging technological trends, and identifies opportunities for improving teaching quality and learner support. Methods An integrative review was conducted using the Whittemore and Knafl framework, with study identification and selection reported in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Of 367 records identified, 21 studies were included. Methodological quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Descriptive and thematic analyses were supplemented by keyword network mapping using VOSviewer version 1.6.20. Results Most studies were multi-authored (71.43%) and published in interdisciplinary education and technology journals (57.14%), with publication activity concentrated in 2024 (28.57%) and 2025 (33.33%). The Western Pacific Region accounted for the largest proportion of studies (38.10%), while no studies originated from the African Region. Teacher performance was the predominant assessment focus ( n = 11; 52.38%), followed by learner behavior ( n = 4; 19.05%) and learner performance ( n = 3; 14.29%). Teacher-focused assessments primarily analyzed learner-generated data using machine learning and natural language processing, whereas some learner-focused assessments employed video-based data and computer vision. Machine learning and natural language processing were the most frequently identified technological approaches ( n = 6), followed by computer vision and multimodal or speech recognition approaches ( n = 3). Most implementations followed a data-input, AI-processing, and output-generation structure, with varying levels of complexity. Thematic analysis identified four domains, while keyword network analysis revealed eight clusters. Discussion The findings highlight a fragmented assessment landscape in which teacher performance and learner behavior are predominantly examined independently. Although learner behavior may provide complementary evidence of teaching effectiveness, reciprocal relationships between teaching and learning remain insufficiently explored. Geographic disparities and methodological heterogeneity further constrain the generalizability and institutional applicability of existing evidence. Conclusion AI offers promising opportunities to strengthen teaching evaluation and learner support in higher education. However, broader geographic representation, methodological rigor, validated assessment frameworks, and equitable, human-supervised implementation are essential to ensure that institutional adoption is guided by robust evidence. Systematic Review Registration https://osf.io/ugt4w .

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.

documents.abstract: Résumé. Le generative engine optimization (GEO) désigne le travail qui vise à faire citer une marque, avec des informations exactes, dans les réponses rédigées par les IA génératives. Cette note décrit la méthode d’audit et d’accompagnement de NEXUS GEO, telle qu’elle est publiée sur son site. L’audit évalue un site et sa présence en ligne selon le Référentiel GEO-47 : 8 piliers, 47 critères, un score global sur 100. Sa grille vaut pour toutes les IA ; la mesure de la présence de la marque porte sur cinq IA (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Mistral et Google AI Overviews), face à trois concurrents nommés. La note présente les trois étapes de la méthode, les indicateurs, les livrables, ce qui est publié et ce qui ne l’est pas, et les limites de la démarche. Abstract. Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the work of getting a brand cited, with accurate information, in answers written by generative AI assistants. This note describes the audit and support method of NEXUS GEO, a French agency, as published on its website. The audit assesses a website and its online presence against the GEO-47 Framework: 8 pillars, 47 criteria and an overall score out of 100. The assessment grid applies to all AI assistants; the brand’s presence is measured on five of them (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Mistral and Google AI Overviews), against three named competitors. The note sets out the three stages of the method, its indicators and deliverables, what is published and what is not, and the method’s limits. Version en ligne, tenue à jour / Online version: https://nexus-geo.fr/methodologie ; Référentiel GEO-47 : https://nexus-geo.fr/referentiel-geo-47

Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes user experiences across digital environments, yet research explaining how AI simultaneously builds and undermines trust remains fragmented. This conceptual chapter introduces the Authenticity Paradox, proposing that AI-enabled personalisation initially enhances perceived authenticity, fostering trust and continued engagement. However, as users become aware of the hidden algorithmic processes underlying personalised interactions, they may reinterpret earlier experiences as engineered rather than genuine, leading to reduced perceived authenticity and declining trust. Drawing on literature from ride-hailing platforms, virtual influencers, and professional AI environments, the chapter develops an integrative conceptual framework demonstrating a common relational mechanism while highlighting context-specific vulnerabilities. The chapter concludes with implications for responsible AI design, transparency, explainability, and future research on trustworthy AI across AI-mediated environments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Stance detection in social media is challenging, as interpreting a text often requires understanding the author's perspective. We re-frame political stance detection as an author-informed text understanding task, where it is desired to infer both the author's political leaning and their stance towards the target from the text. We first show that human annotators struggle to infer authors' political leanings and stances from individual tweets, and that pretrained large language models (LLMs) perform below human level in this setting. We then demonstrate that author context improves stance detection for both humans and LLMs, with particularly pronounced benefits for tweets perceived as sarcastic. Through extensive experiments, we further show that LLMs can be effectively fine-tuned to predict authors' political affiliations, and that author-informed fine-tuning yields better stance detection performance than standard fine-tuning. This approach not only surpasses human performance but also improves generalization across datasets. To support further research on author-informed political stance detection, we release a large dataset of stance-labeled tweets enriched with author-context information.

BACKGROUND: The microcolony multiplex opsonophagocytic killing assay (mMOPA) is a critical functional assay for evaluating pneumococcal vaccine immunogenicity; however, its colony-counting readout is scientist-dependent and time‑consuming. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: In this study, we developed and optimized a deep learning model (DLM) colony-counting tool by adapting the Segment Anything (SAM) foundation model and evaluated its performance using historical assay qualification datasets spanning 12 pneumococcal serotypes, with additional benchmarking against blinded human expert counts. RESULTS: The DLM-derived counts demonstrated strong correlation and agreement with both historical CTL ImmunoSpot® counts and expert counts. Notably, DLM outperformed CTL for a challenging serotype and produced comparable opsonophagocytic titers with those generated using CTL counts within the representative samples evaluated. These results establish the DLM approach as fit for purpose for mMOPA readouts. CONCLUSIONS: Overall, this work removes a key throughput bottleneck in mMOPA, enables a "walkaway" colony-counting workflow supporting improved operational efficiency and scalability for large clinical studies, and highlights the broader value of integrating bioanalytical expertise with modern computer vision to advance scalable, image-based bioassays in vaccine and drug development.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: To rigorously establish the value of a novel deep learning method, it must be compared against appropriate baselines. As deep learning has become increasingly common in the physical and life sciences, there have been numerous cases in which apparent progress has turned out to be an artifact of omitted or missing baselines. In this work, we investigate whether this problem can be mitigated by using large language models to automate the construction of baselines. We assemble 36 supervised classification and regression tasks from peer-reviewed studies in Nature, Science, and Cell-family journals that investigate novel deep learning methods for scientific applications. We then use a language model to construct simple baselines for each task. These automatically constructed baselines are strong, recovering a median of 95.5% (mean 85.7%) of the gap between a trivial predictor and the score of the deep learning model. The median simple baseline matches or exceeds the performance of the deep learning model in 12 studies. We further examine the variation across scientific domains and publication venues and we characterize the effects of test-time compute and access to different levels of study context. As human peer review has struggled to keep up with the rapidly increasing volume of research articles in recent years, our results suggest that automated baseline construction is a practical and scalable check on deep learning contributions in the physical and life sciences.

Radiology is adopting artificial intelligence (AI) faster than it is studying what AI does to radiologists' perceptual expertise and interpretive skill. The question has partly shifted from whether these tools perform well on benchmark tasks to what happens to clinical judgment when use of these tools becomes routine. Two risks accompany this transition: automation bias, the tendency to follow AI suggestions without adequate scrutiny, and deskilling, the erosion of perceptual and interpretive ability through disuse, typically revealed when AI support is withdrawn. Incorrect AI output degrades accuracy regardless of experience, the benefit of assistance varies unpredictably across readers and tasks, and performance falls after AI withdrawal; neither risk has been studied longitudinally in radiology. A confidence-stratified triage model is proposed in which calibrated AI confidence, not findings alone, routes cases to low-, intermediate-, or high-confidence streams: output withheld until independent reading, shown with uncertainty signals and a checklist, or shown with random blinded audit. Demonstrated local confidence calibration is a precondition for deployment, and stream thresholds and audit rates should be weighted by task and potential clinical harm, not error probability alone. Rather than applying one workflow to every case, the model redistributes radiologist attention to where AI error is most likely and most consequential, operationalizing four principles: keeping the radiologist in the decision loop, making AI uncertainty visible, inserting targeted cognitive friction, and governing the human-AI interaction as a system. A research agenda to determine whether these countermeasures reduce automation bias and skill erosion in practice is also proposed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Quantum materials exhibit diverse electronic and functional phenomena, but their characterization requires extensive experimental expertise, iterative decision-making and accumulated laboratory knowledge that is difficult to document and transfer. Here we introduce Quantum Agent (QUANTA), an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for autonomous quantum-materials characterization. Using a widely adopted Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS) as an experimental platform, QUANTA combines retrieval augmentation using scientific literature, experimental protocols and prior measurements with specialized agents for experimental planning, troubleshooting, and data interpretation. A separate deterministic control layer validates instrument actions. Guided by incoming data, QUANTA evaluates measurement quality, revises experimental plans and selects subsequent measurements. We demonstrate these capabilities through transport measurements of the topological Weyl semimetal TaP, as well as investigations of nonlinear responses in magnetic material Co2MnGa. These results establish QUANTA as a generalizable framework for evidence-driven, safeguarded and closed-loop quantum-materials characterization.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education offers transformative opportunities, particularly for inclusive classrooms where students with diverse needs require adaptive and supportive technologies. Despite this advancement, there is limited understanding of how prepared pre-service special educators are to use AI tools effectively. This study addresses this gap by examining the awareness, readiness, and AI-related competencies of pre-service special educators in India. The research specifically investigates their awareness, readiness and technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge (TPACK) and explores differences based on demographic factors such as gender, level of professional training (B.Ed. vs M.Ed.), and prior exposure to AI. A descriptive and inferential quantitative research design was adopted, utilizing a structured questionnaire administered to 200 pre-service special educators. Data analysis included descriptive statistics, t-tests, ANOVA, and correlation to identify trends and associations. Findings revealed moderate levels of awareness and readiness, with significant differences linked to demographic variables and prior training. Notably, higher TPACK scores were strongly associated with greater readiness to adopt AI. These results have practical implications for teacher education programs, suggesting the need for targeted AI training and curriculum enhancements to equip future special educators for inclusive, technology-rich learning environments.

Healthcare professionals work within complex and demanding environments characterised by substantial responsibility, emotional demands, high workloads, exposure to distressing and potentially traumatic events, and persistent workforce pressures (Hansel et al., 2024; Patel et al., 2018; Sattar et al., 2024). These occupational demands can affect healthcare workers’ psychological and emotional wellbeing and highlight the importance of accessible and appropriate support mechanisms within healthcare settings. Despite increasing recognition of healthcare worker wellbeing as an important workforce and organisational priority, healthcare professionals may be reluctant to access formal psychological or mental health services (Gold et al., 2016; Trusty et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025; Young et al., 2025). Peer support represents one alternative or complementary approach. Existing evidence suggests that peer support may help reduce feelings of isolation, strengthen resilience, and support emotional wellbeing and adaptive coping among healthcare professionals (Walker & Peterson, 2021; Watson, 2019). However, peer-support initiatives vary considerably in their purpose, structure, mode of delivery, target populations, level of formality, and organisational context. Consequently, there is a need to systematically map the existing evidence. This scoping review aims to map the existing literature on peer support among healthcare professionals, care staff, and non-clinical healthcare staff, with particular attention to the characteristics of peer-support approaches and the barriers and facilitators influencing their implementation, access, uptake, and engagement. The review will also identify gaps in the current evidence and areas requiring further research.

Abstract The silent cry for help is often a voice that is faint and hesitant, particularly for Black males in community colleges. Stigmas tied to their identity and cultural challenges that arise before they even arrive on campus contribute to the difficulties they face. This chapter explores the unique challenges confronting Black male students, highlighting barriers created by traditional educational structures and the lack of culturally responsive approaches. It underscores how eurocentric curricula and teacher-centered methods fail to meet the need for autonomy, competence, and relatedness creating gaps in connecting, communicating, and discovering. Emphasizing self-determination, the chapter illustrates how intrinsic motivation, and tailored support can empower Black males. It also discusses the role of mentoring and coaching, as well as alternative learning environments that align with the cultural and social contexts. Overall, it calls for a reimagining of higher education to create inclusive and equitable spaces for Black male students.

Generative AI now produces images and poems that people cannot reliably distinguish from human-made work, so people often judge for themselves who made a work. We examine how these perceived-authorship judgments relate to aesthetic preference. In a public online AI Art Turing Test, 11,123 people judged whether each of 50 pictures (26 AI-generated) was made by a human and were asked for their favourite. Among the 9,152 respondents who judged their favourite, a picture was 22.1 percentage points more likely to be judged human-made when it was the respondent's favourite, holding respondent and picture fixed. The association was similar for AI-generated and human-made favourites, was positive for all 50 pictures, and appeared under every reported detection strategy. Respondents most negative about AI art chose fewer AI-generated favourites (47% against 60% among the most positive) but more often believed them human-made, partly because others also judged those pictures human. As a result, in every opinion group a third to two fifths of respondents named an AI-generated favourite they believed human-made. A reanalysis of a published experiment on AI-generated poetry, in which 230 people rated each poem before judging its authorship, found the same pattern, although the AI poems were rated higher. When provenance is hidden, liking and perceived human authorship travel together, consistent with aesthetic response serving as evidence of a human maker and with beliefs about the maker shaping enjoyment. The findings qualify research on bias against AI art, which typically uses explicit labels, and inform AI disclosure policy.

The intersection of artificial intelligence and behavioral finance presents an underexplored but commercially significant terrain for reimagining how tourism firms design and implement their pricing strategies. While revenue management in travel and hospitality has long depended on demand-based algorithmic models a persistent gap between what these systems predict and what consumers actually do reveals a structural blind spot the systematic cognitive biases that shape purchase decisions in ways that rational utility models simply cannot capture. This chapter develops a behavioral-AI pricing framework by synthesizing prospect theory mental accounting reference price anchoring and social proof mechanisms within the architecture of modern machine learning revenue management systems. Drawing on secondary evidence from major online travel platforms and published booking behavior studies we demonstrate that tourism consumers exhibit consistent loss aversion effects when exposed to dynamic price fluctuations that reference price anchoring significantly modulates willingness to pay at different stages of the booking funnel and that AI pricing engines which ignore these behavioral dimensions routinely suppress conversion or trigger demand destruction. Our proposed framework integrates behavioral signals into AI feature engineering arguing that affective pricing cues cancellation-loss framing and social validation mechanisms can be systematically deployed to improve both conversion rates and revenue per available unit without exploiting consumers in ethically problematic ways. The chapter contributes to the growing literature on neuroeconomic applications in hospitality management while offering practical direction to revenue managers who seek to humanize not merely automate their pricing decisions.

Abstract Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is important for interpreting transformer-based models, yet explanation quality in Arabic language remains underexplored. This work presents a comprehensive benchmark of attribution XAI methods for Arabic sentiment analysis and hate speech detection, evaluating LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, DeepLIFT, and ensemble variants across three Arabic transformer models. We assess explanations using faithfulness and plausibility metrics and complement score-based faithfulness evaluation with rank-based aggregation via Borda count. We show that selective ensembling yields a statistically significant but modest improvement over individual XAI methods in faithfulness, with LIME+SHAP improving the primary Combined score by an average paired difference of approximately 0.012 over LIME in sentiment classification. The same general trend persists under cross-task evaluation on hate-speech detection. In contrast, ensemble configurations provide little improvement in agreement with human-annotated rationales, demonstrating that improved model-centered faithfulness does not necessarily translate to human-centered plausibility. We additionally introduce a parameter-free, automated rationale-selection method based on elbow-detection that achieves competitive faithfulness with lower computational cost. Overall, the study provides a rigorous, reproducible benchmark and practical guidance for efficient and reliable XAI in Arabic NLP. The code to reproduce the benchmark is available at: \url{https://github.com/ychafiqui/arabic_xai_benchmark}

Abstract Introduction Medical Artificial Intelligence (MAI) is transforming healthcare but raises significant ethical concerns. Despite emerging principles and regulations, to our knowledge, no standardized clinical bioethics framework exists to guide MAI practice. Objective This Delphi study sought global expert agreement on ethical challenges, principles, guidelines, and practical tools for MAI use. Method A four-round international eDelphi study, conducted under ACCORD and DELPHISTAR guidance, engaged multidisciplinary stakeholders identified through systematic review and targeted recruitment. Preliminary items were evidence-derived and iteratively refined. Consensus (≥ 80% agreement across two rounds) was predefined. Surveys were anonymized and randomized. Ethical approval and protocol registration were secured before study initiation. Results The panel included 53 participants from 21 countries. Survey rounds started November 2025 and ended February 2026. 170 items were considered. 132 reached consensus. Items were classified into bioethical issues, values, principles, solutions, a checklist for clinicians, and report markers for risk management. Discussion This study produced clinician-focused practice guidelines for the bioethical use of MAI. Ethical components aligned with prior literature, while no new bioethical principles met consensus. Limitations included geographic imbalance and stakeholder representation. Recommendations emphasized human responsibility, governance, and practical implementation tools. Conclusion This Delphi consensus provides practical, ethics-based guidance for the responsible integration of MAI into clinical practice and institutional governance.
